profile.name: Okayama
profile.tagline: A Muromachi-period Japanese kōwaka-mai about Yoshitsune's retainers' families
profile.insight: Okayama is a single surviving kōwaka-mai manuscript from the Muromachi period, telling the story of Yoshitsune's retainers' bereaved families at a hut in Okayama.
profile.profile: Okayama is a Japanese kōwaka-mai dance-drama from the Muromachi period, belonging to the hōgan-mono genre focused on Minamoto no Yoshitsune. It narrates the story of the families of two retainers, Satō Tsugunobu and Satō Tadanobu, after their deaths. The dance is performed as a narrative with a libretto surviving in a single manuscript, linking to the Gikeiki chronicle and paired with the kōwaka Yashima. The story culminates in the widows and relatives building a hut in Okayama and dying peacefully together.
profile.profile_long: Okayama is a kōwaka-mai, a form of Japanese dance-drama that flourished during the Muromachi period (1336–1573). It belongs to the hōgan-mono genre, which centers on the legendary 12th-century military commander Minamoto no Yoshitsune, who held the title of hōgan (captain of the guard). The dance narrates a poignant episode following the deaths of two of Yoshitsune's retainers, Satō Tsugunobu and Satō Tadanobu. The story unfolds at Takadachi, where Nikō, a noblewoman turned nun and mother of the fallen retainers, implores Yoshitsune to become the eboshi-oya (guardian) for the two brothers' fatherless children. Yoshitsune consents, sponsoring their genpuku (coming-of-age) ceremony and naming them Yoshinobu and Yoshitada. The children are welcomed into the household of Fujiwara no Hidehira, a prominent regional lord. Meanwhile, the widows of Tsugunobu and Tadanobu, aided by the warrior monk Musashibō Benkei, take religious vows and join Nikō on a pilgrimage through Mutsu Province. Their journey ends at a place called Okayama, where they build a hut and eventually pass away peacefully together. This kōwaka-mai is closely linked to another work, Yashima, and together they form a narrative often referred to as the "Tale of Nikō." The text of Okayama has been connected to a passage in the Gikeiki, a medieval chronicle of Yoshitsune's life, with book eight containing a nearly identical section to the first half of the dance's libretto. The libretto survives in a single manuscript known as the Bunroku-bon, copied by Ueyama Munehisa and held by the Tenri Central Library, which also published a facsimile edition. The dance likely would have been performed with narrative chanting and stylized movement typical of kōwaka-mai, though specific performance techniques are not detailed in surviving sources. The story's focus on bereavement, religious devotion, and filial duty reflects the cultural values of the Muromachi period and the enduring legacy of Yoshitsune in Japanese performing arts.

sections.origins_and_history: Okayama is a kōwaka-mai from the Muromachi period, a Japanese dance-drama genre. It belongs to the hōgan-mono category, which dramatizes episodes related to Minamoto no Yoshitsune, a 12th-century military leader. The libretto survives in a single manuscript, the Bunroku-bon, held by Tenri Central Library. The dance's text is linked to the Gikeiki chronicle and is considered a sequel to the kōwaka Yashima.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance tells the story of bereaved relatives of Yoshitsune's retainers, focusing on themes of guardianship, pilgrimage, and religious devotion. It likely served to commemorate these figures and their virtues within the cultural context of Muromachi Japan.
sections.notable_figures: Minamoto no Yoshitsune, Satō Tsugunobu, Satō Tadanobu, Nikō (the noblewoman turned nun), Fujiwara no Hidehira, Musashibō Benkei, Ueyama Munehisa (copyist of the manuscript).
sections.lineage: Okayama is part of the hōgan-mono genre of kōwaka-mai, paired narratively with Yashima. The text relates closely to the Gikeiki chronicle, forming a linked tradition of Yoshitsune-related stories.

claims.text: The widows become nuns and travel as pilgrims around Mutsu Province until they come to Okayama, where they build a hut and die peacefully together.
claims.quote: Tsugunobu and Tadanobu's widows become nuns with the assistance of Musashibō Benkei, and the two women join their mother-in-law Nikō and travel as pilgrims around Mutsu Province until they come to a place called Okayama, where they build a hut and die peacefully together.
